hook: The farmer turned general who beheaded a king and ruled England as Lord Protector.

pages.x: Oliver Cromwell was born in Huntingdon in 1599, into a family of minor gentry. In his thirties he went through a religious crisis and became a passionate Puritan, sure that God was guiding his life. He sat in Parliament for Cambridge.
King Charles I believed kings were chosen by God and ruled for eleven years without calling Parliament. In 1642 civil war broke out between the king's Cavaliers and Parliament's Roundheads.

Cromwell, who had no military training, raised a cavalry regiment, the Ironsides, chosen for faith and discipline. He helped build the New Model Army, which crushed the king's forces at Naseby in 1645.

Charles kept plotting. In January 1649 he was tried for treason and beheaded outside the Banqueting House in London. Cromwell was the third of 59 men to sign the death warrant. England became a republic.
In 1649 he invaded Ireland. At Drogheda and Wexford his troops massacred thousands of soldiers, priests and townspeople. In Ireland his name is still remembered with hatred.

In 1653 he threw out Parliament, telling it: "You have sat too long for any good you have been doing", and became Lord Protector, king in all but name. He refused the crown. Theatres were closed, and Jews were allowed back into England after 365 years.

He told the painter of his portrait to paint him as he really was, "warts and everything". After he died in 1658 the monarchy returned, and his body was dug up and hanged. His head was stuck on a pole above Westminster Hall for over 20 years.

Cromwell is one of the most argued-over figures in British history: a champion of Parliament to some, a dictator and king-killer to others, and in Ireland a butcher. After him, no English king could rule without Parliament.
pts: Led Parliament's army in the English Civil War
Ruled as Lord Protector of a republic
Signed the death warrant of King Charles I
